etymology: From bed and the Old English stede, “a place, a standing, that whereon a thing stands”; hence the frame that bears a bed. In the KJV it occurs but once, of the iron bedstead of Og king of Bashan.
biblical_def: A bedstead is the frame or standing-place of a bed — the bedframe, as distinguished from the bedding laid upon it. The word occurs once only in all the Authorized Version, and it is a hapax with a giant in it: “For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants; behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron… nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it, after the cubit of a man” (Deu 3:11). Moses is writing history, not fable. Og was a real king who came out to real battle at Edrei (Deu 3:1), whose coast is surveyed among the conquered lands (Jos 12:4), and whose overthrow Israel sang for a mercy that endureth for ever. He was of the remnant of the Rephaim, and his iron bedframe — some thirteen feet by six — was kept at Rabbath of the children of Ammon as a relic any man might go and measure. The Spirit gives the dimensions precisely because the thing could be checked. The bedstead preaches two doctrines at once. First, that the LORD is not hindered by stature: the giant whose bedframe was a wonder fell before a people who had no iron at all, for the battle is the LORD’s. Second, that greatness of body is no defence against the judgment of God. Og lay down at last on a bed he could not carry with him, and the iron frame outlived the king who slept on it.
webster_summary: The frame or standing-place that bears a bed; in Deuteronomy, the iron bedframe of Og king of Bashan.
webster_full: BEDSTEAD, a frame for supporting a bed; the standing-place of a bed.
From bed and the Saxon stede, “a place, a standing.”
A KJV hapax, occurring but once (Deu 3:11).
Og’s bedstead was of iron, nine cubits long and four broad, kept at Rabbath.
It witnesses to the real stature of a real king of the Rephaim.
scriptures: Deu 3:11

For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants; behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron; is it not in Rabbath of the children of Ammon? nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it, after the cubit of a man.
Deu 3:1
Then we turned, and went up the way to Bashan: and Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.
Jos 12:4
And the coast of Og king of Bashan, which was of the remnant of the giants, that dwelt at Ashtaroth and at Edrei,
Amo 6:4
That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall;
corruption_summary: The live misuse is the reflex that files Og among legends because his bedstead was nine cubits long; Moses gives the measurements precisely because the thing could be measured.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live misuse here, and it is the modern reflex that hears “nine cubits” and quietly reclassifies Og as folklore, a giant borrowed from the tales of the nations and dressed in Israelite clothes. The canonical narrative does not permit it. Moses names the king, the kingdom, the city of the battle, the tribe he sprang from, and the town where the relic was kept — is it not in Rabbath of the children of Ammon? — and then gives the length and the breadth after the common cubit of a man, the very details a man supplies when he expects to be checked. Joshua surveys Og’s coast among the lands actually taken; the psalms sing his fall among the LORD’s real mercies. To call this legend is not humility before the evidence; it is unbelief dressed as caution. The spade of the archaeologist may corroborate Scripture, but it never sits in judgment on Scripture: the Word of God is the authority, and the dust is the witness.

The second temptation runs the other way — to make Og a curiosity, a wonder for the museum, and to miss the doctrine in the bedframe. The Spirit did not record the iron for our amusement. Israel had no iron and no stature, and the LORD delivered the giant into their hand, that no flesh should glory in His presence. And Og, whose bedstead was a marvel to measure, died like a man and left his frame behind him. Amos knew the same lesson from the other end: they that lie upon beds of ivory and stretch themselves upon their couches shall go captive with the first that go captive. Whether the bed be iron or ivory, no man carries it through the judgment, and the LORD who felled the last of the Rephaim is not impressed by the size of anyone.
roots_summary: The word means the frame or standing-place that bears a bed.
roots_lines: Bedstead — from bed + Old English stede, “a place, a standing.”
It denotes the frame that bears the bed, not the bedding itself.
A KJV hapax, occurring only in Deu 3:11.
Og’s was of iron, nine cubits by four, kept as a relic at Rabbath.
It witnesses to a real king of the Rephaim, really judged by God.
usage: Og’s bedstead was of iron, nine cubits long — Moses gives the measure because it could be measured.
The giant fell before a people without iron: the battle is the LORD’s, not the tallest man’s.
Iron bed or ivory couch, no man carries his bedstead through the judgment of God.

etymology: From good + man, an old English title for the master of a household — the husband, the householder, the man who owns the house and answers for it. In the KJV it commonly stands in the phrase “the goodman of the house.”
biblical_def: The goodman is the master of the house — not a man who is morally good, but the householder, the head of the family, the owner who answers for what happens under his roof. Solomon uses it of the husband away on business: “the goodman is not at home, he is gone a long journey” (Pro 7:19), the adulteress’s excuse for her sin. In the parables it is the man who hires the labourers and against whom the murmurers grumble (Mat 20:11); in the upper room it is the householder to whom the disciples must say, “The Master saith, Where is the guestchamber?” (Mar 14:14). But the word’s weight falls on our Lord’s watchword: “if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken up” (Mat 24:43; so Luk 12:39). Here is a doctrine of order and a doctrine of vigilance together. Christ assumes a man over the house, responsible for its keeping — the creational headship Scripture everywhere assumes, and which the church must not surrender. And He assumes that the hour is unknown. The whole point of the figure is that the goodman was not told which watch; had he known, he would have sat up. Because he does not know, he must watch always. Every Christian householder is a goodman under the great Householder, keeping his house against a coming he cannot date and must not miss.
webster_summary: The master of a house; the householder, the head of a family; not one who is morally good but the man who owns and answers for the house.
webster_full: GOODMAN, the master of a house or family; a householder; the husband.
From good and man, an old title of the head of a household.
It does not mean a man of good morals but the owner of the house.
The goodman is not at home, he is gone a long journey (Pro 7:19).
Christ’s watchword: the goodman knew not in what watch the thief would come (Mat 24:43).
scriptures: And when they had received it, they murmured against the goodman of the house,
But know this, that if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken up.
And wheresoever he shall go in, say ye to the goodman of the house, The Master saith, Where is the guestchamber, where I shall eat the passover with my disciples?
And this know, that if the goodman of the house had known what hour the thief would come, he would have watched, and not have suffered his house to be broken through.
corruption_summary: A live misuse: the watchfulness Christ commands is traded for date-setting, which is the very thing the figure forbids — the goodman was not told the watch.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a live misuse, and it is worth naming plainly. Our Lord’s figure of the goodman turns wholly on ignorance of the hour: if he had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched. He did not know. Therefore he must watch always. Yet the popular prophecy industry of the last two centuries has done the opposite with the very text — charting the watch, dating the coming, printing the year, and calling that watchfulness. It is not. It is the goodman deciding he knows the hour and going to bed for the other three watches. The date-setting habit is a fruit of the dispensational system Darby and Scofield bequeathed to the modern church, a scheme unknown to any Reformation confession; and every failed date it has produced has made the world laugh at the blessed hope. Christ did not give a timetable. He gave a charge: watch, for ye know neither the day nor the hour.

The word also guards an order the age would like to dissolve. The goodman of the house is the man of the house, the householder responsible for its keeping, and Christ frames His parable on that assumption as on solid ground — as Scripture does everywhere, setting the husband as head of the wife and the father as the one who answers for his household before God. To sneer at the very notion of a man over a house is to quarrel not with an old English word but with the creational order the Lord Himself takes for granted. Recover both halves: let the Christian man own his charge as the goodman under the great Householder, and let him keep his house awake, for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh.
roots_summary: The word means the master of a house, the householder who owns and answers for it.
roots_lines: Goodman — from good + man, an old title of the householder.
It denotes the master of the house, the husband, the head of the family.
It carries no sense of moral goodness; it names an office, not a character.
In the parables it is the householder who hires, owns, and answers (Mat 20:11).
Christ makes him the figure of the watchful saint who knows not the hour (Mat 24:43).
usage: The goodman of the house is the master of it — the office, not a verdict on his morals.
Had the goodman known the watch, he would have watched: he was not told, so he watches always.
Say ye to the goodman of the house, The Master saith — even the upper room was asked of its head.

etymology: From fire + brand, from the Old English brand, “a burning, a piece of burning wood”; hence a stick snatched out of the fire, half-consumed and still smoking.
biblical_def: A firebrand is a piece of burning wood — a stick out of the hearth, charred, smoking, half-eaten by the flame. Scripture uses it three ways. It is a picture of a spent threat: Isaiah bids Ahaz “fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands” (Isa 7:4), for Rezin and Pekah, who terrified Judah, were burnt-out stumps with nothing left but smoke. It is a picture of reckless sin: “as a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death” (Pro 26:18), so is the man who deceives his neighbour and says he was only jesting. But the word rises to its glory in the third use. Amos says of a spared remnant, “ye were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning” (Amo 4:11) — and Zechariah hears the LORD say the same over Joshua the high priest, standing in filthy garments with Satan at his right hand to resist him: “The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan… is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?” (Zec 3:2). Then the filthy garments are taken away and a change of raiment given (Zec 3:4). This is justification, and there is no plainer picture of it in the Old Testament. The accuser accuses truly; the brand is genuinely filthy; and God does not answer Satan by denying the charge but by rebuking the accuser, removing the iniquity, and clothing the man in a righteousness not his own.
webster_summary: A piece of burning wood; a stick snatched from the fire, half-consumed and smoking; in Amos and Zechariah, a figure of the sinner plucked from judgment.
webster_full: FIREBRAND, a piece of wood kindled or on fire; a brand out of the burning.
From fire and Old English brand, “a burning, a burning stick.”
Figuratively, a spent enemy: two tails of smoking firebrands (Isa 7:4).
Figuratively, reckless mischief, cast about by a mad man (Pro 26:18).
Chiefly, the sinner plucked from the fire by the hand of God (Amo 4:11; Zec 3:2).
scriptures: Amo 4:11
I have overthrown some of you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and ye were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD.
Zec 3:2
And the LORD said unto Satan, The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan; even the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee: is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?
Zec 3:4

And he answered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying, Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment.
Isa 7:4
And say unto him, Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a burnt stick out of the hearth; it recovers justification by grace alone — the brand does not pluck itself out of the fire.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes every scheme of salvation in which the sinner contributes. Set the scene of Zechariah’s third chapter and let it preach: Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the LORD in filthy garments, and Satan stands at his right hand to resist him. The accusation is not false. The garments are really filthy; the high priest of a returned and guilty people has nothing to plead. And the LORD does not answer the accuser by disputing the charge. He answers, “The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan… is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?” The whole defence of the guilty man is that God has already laid a hand on him and pulled him out. Then comes the double work of justification in two sentences: “I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee” — the filthy garments taken away, guilt removed — “and I will clothe thee with change of raiment” — a righteousness imputed, not woven by the wearer. Grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, in one vision.

Mark the monergism of the figure, for it is the whole point. A brand does not pluck itself out of the fire. It has no hand to reach with and no will to reach; it lies in the coals and burns, and it will burn to ashes unless another hand comes into the flame and snatches it. The brand cannot even want to be plucked until it is out. So Amos says to the remnant, ye were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning — passive, acted upon, saved by a hand not their own. Yet mark also the rebuke that follows: “yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD.” Men snatched from the burning and unmoved by it are the saddest sight in Scripture. If God has plucked you out, do not lie there smoking as though nothing had happened; the hand that saved you calls you home.
roots_summary: The word means a piece of burning wood, a stick snatched from the fire.
roots_lines: Firebrand — from fire + Old English brand, “a burning stick.”
It denotes wood half-consumed, charred and smoking, out of the hearth.
It figures a spent enemy, all smoke and no flame (Isa 7:4).
It figures reckless mischief cast about by a mad man (Pro 26:18).
Chiefly it figures the sinner plucked out of the burning by God (Zec 3:2).
usage: Ye were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning — and the brand did not pluck itself.
Is not this a brand plucked out of the fire? The LORD rebukes the accuser and clothes the accused.
Fear not the two tails of these smoking firebrands: a spent enemy is smoke without flame.

etymology: The old past tense of seethe, from the Old English sēoþan, “to boil”; hence sod, boiled, and the past participle sodden, boiled through. It has no kinship with the modern noun for turf, nor any with Sodom.
biblical_def: Sod is the old past tense of seethe, to boil — not turf, and no kin to Sodom. To sod a thing was to boil it in water; the past participle survives in sodden, boiled through. Its first appearance carries the ruin of a birthright: “And Jacob sod pottage: and Esau came from the field, and he was faint” (Gen 25:29). A pot of boiled lentiles bought the double portion and the covenant line, and the Holy Ghost fixes the verdict for ever: Esau was a “profane person… who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright” (Heb 12:16). Profane means common — the man who could not tell the difference between what is holy and what is only hot, and traded eternity for a bellyful. The word’s other great use is a lesson in worship. Of the passover the LORD commanded: “Eat not of it raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire” (Exo 12:9). God did not merely require the lamb; He required the manner of its dressing, and boiling it was forbidden. Josiah’s reformers kept the distinction exactly: “they roasted the passover with fire according to the ordinance: but the other holy offerings sod they in pots” (2Ch 35:13). Here is the regulative principle in a cooking pot. What God commands is required; what He has not commanded is not permitted; and the difference between roast and sodden is not a triviality when the LORD Himself has spoken to it.
webster_summary: The old past tense of seethe, to boil; hence sodden, boiled through. Not turf, and no kin to Sodom.
webster_full: SOD, the preterit of seethe; boiled.
From the Saxon sēoþan, “to boil, to seethe”; participle sodden.
Wholly distinct from the modern noun for turf, and from Sodom.
Jacob sod pottage, and Esau sold his birthright for it (Gen 25:29).
The passover was not to be sodden with water, but roast with fire (Exo 12:9).
scriptures: And Jacob sod pottage: and Esau came from the field, and he was faint:
Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.
Exo 12:9
Eat not of it raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire; his head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof.
And they roasted the passover with fire according to the ordinance: but the other holy offerings sod they in pots, and in caldrons, and in pans, and divided them speedily among all the people.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old past tense of seethe; it recovers Esau’s profanity and the LORD’s right to command the manner of His own worship.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the profane heart — and profane, in Scripture’s sense, does not mean foul-mouthed but common, unable to tell the holy from the ordinary. Jacob sod pottage; Esau came in from the field faint, smelled the boiling lentiles, and sold the birthright of the covenant line for a bowl of it. He did not deny God; he simply could not see why a promise five hundred years off should outweigh a hot meal now. Hebrews names him for ever a profane person who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright, and warns the church to look diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God after his pattern. Every generation has its pottage — the hot, immediate, steaming thing that costs only an inheritance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God commands the manner of His own worship. The LORD did not only appoint the passover lamb; He appointed how it should be dressed — not raw, not sodden at all with water, but roast with fire, head and legs and purtenance. A man might reasonably ask what difference boiling makes; the answer is that the LORD has spoken, and that ends it. Josiah’s reformers kept the line to the letter, roasting the passover with fire according to the ordinance while the other holy offerings they sod in pots. This is the regulative principle in a kitchen: what God commands in His worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not ours to add, however sensible it seems in the pot.
roots_summary: The word is the old past tense of seethe, to boil in water.
roots_lines: Sod — the preterit of seethe, Old English sēoþan, “to boil.”
Its participle is sodden, boiled through (Exo 12:9).
It is no kin to the modern noun for turf, nor to the city of Sodom.
Jacob sod pottage, and Esau despised his birthright for it (Gen 25:29).
The passover might be roast but never sodden — God rules His own worship.
usage: Jacob sod pottage — and a bowl of boiled lentiles bought away a birthright.
Eat not of it sodden at all with water, but roast with fire: the LORD appoints the manner.
Josiah roasted the passover according to the ordinance, and sod the other offerings in pots.

etymology: From draw, with the old spelling of the verbal noun; hence that which is drawn — a drawing of a net and its catch, and also a drawing away, whence the “draught house” or privy. It is an entirely different word from drought, dryness.
biblical_def: A draught is a drawing — that which is drawn — and the KJV carries the word in two senses that stand far apart. The first is the fisherman’s: “Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught” (Luk 5:4). Peter had toiled all night and taken nothing; at Christ’s word he let down the nets and enclosed so great a multitude of fishes that the net brake and two ships began to sink. And Peter’s response to the miracle is the whole gospel in a sentence: he “fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luk 5:8). Nearness to Christ does not flatter a man; it undoes him. The draught did not make Peter feel successful, it made him feel unclean — and the Lord who would not depart made him a fisher of men. The second sense is the drawing away of what the body voids: the draught, the privy, the sink. Our Lord uses it to end a controversy: what enters the mouth “goeth out into the draught, purging all meats” (Mar 7:19), for defilement is not in the food but in the heart. And Jehu “brake down the house of Baal, and made it a draught house unto this day” (2Ki 10:27) — the idol’s temple turned into a latrine, the LORD’s contempt for false gods made architecture. One word, two draughts: the net that catches men, and the sink that carries filth away.
webster_summary: That which is drawn: the drawing of a net and its catch; also a drawing away, whence the draught house or privy. Wholly distinct from drought, dryness.
webster_full: DRAUGHT, the act of drawing; that which is drawn; a net full drawn out of the water.
From the verb draw; it has no kinship with drought, want of rain.
Let down your nets for a draught — the fisherman’s catch (Luk 5:4).
Also the drawing away of the body’s waste; hence the draught house, a privy (2Ki 10:27).
Christ used the second sense to prove that defilement is of the heart (Mar 7:19).
scriptures: Luk 5:4
Now when he had left speaking, he said unto Simon, Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught.
Luk 5:8
When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.
Mar 7:19
Because it entereth not into his heart, but into the belly, and goeth out into the draught, purging all meats?
And they brake down the image of Baal, and brake down the house of Baal, and made it a draught house unto this day.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but an old word for a drawing, in two far-apart senses; it recovers that defilement is of the heart and that Christ’s nearness humbles before it commissions.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the religion of the outside. Christ’s hearers had built a whole system on what a man might put in his mouth, and He undid it with the plainest of arguments: meat entereth not into the heart but into the belly, and goeth out into the draught — purging all meats. The stomach is not the seat of holiness and the sink is not a moral judge. Defilement comes out of the heart: evil thoughts, adulteries, murders, thefts, blasphemies. Every age rebuilds the same system with a fresh menu, scrubbing the outside of the cup and reckoning itself clean; and every age must be told again that the fountain is within.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what a draught of fishes does to a man. Peter had fished all night and caught nothing, which is a fisherman’s humiliation; then at a carpenter’s word he took so many that the nets brake. He did not boast of the haul. He fell down at Jesus’ knees and said, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord. That is what the presence of Christ does: it does not confirm a man in his own estimate, it strips him. And the Lord whom he begged to depart did not depart, but said, Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men. Grace meets the man who has just discovered he cannot bear it, and sends him out to draw the same net over the world.
roots_summary: The word means a drawing — a net drawn out with its catch, or a drawing away of filth.
roots_lines: Draught — from draw; that which is drawn.
It is a wholly different word from drought, dryness or want of rain.
In the gospels, the drawing of the nets and the fishes taken (Luk 5:4).
Also the drawing away of waste; hence the draught house, a privy (2Ki 10:27).
Christ used it to teach that defilement proceeds from the heart (Mar 7:19).
usage: Launch out into the deep and let down your nets for a draught — and Peter’s net brake.
The great draught did not puff Peter up; it laid him at Christ’s knees, a sinful man.
Jehu made the house of Baal a draught house — the LORD’s contempt for idols in stone.

etymology: From the Old English slīm, “slime, mire”; in the KJV it renders the Hebrew word for bitumen or asphalt — the natural pitch that seeps out of the ground in Mesopotamia and about the Salt Sea, used anciently as mortar and as waterproofing.
biblical_def: Slime in the Authorized Version is not pond scum but bitumen — the black asphalt that oozes from the earth in Mesopotamia and about the vale of Siddim, used by the ancients for mortar and for caulking. It appears at the two ends of a great contrast. At Babel the builders said “one to another, Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly. And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter” (Gen 11:3), and with that brick and slime they undertook a tower “whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name” (Gen 11:4). Here is man’s religion in one verse: a manufactured stone, a manufactured mortar, a self-made stair to God, and a name of his own getting. The LORD came down, confounded the tongue, and called the place Babel (Gen 11:9). But the same slime appears again in gentler hands: when Moses’ mother could hide him no longer, “she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein” (Exo 2:3), and the pitch of the earth kept the water out and the deliverer alive. The identical substance builds the tower of rebellion and seals the ark of salvation. What men gather to make themselves a name, God takes up to save His people; and the difference is never in the tar but in whose hand is spreading it.
webster_summary: Bitumen or asphalt; the natural pitch of the ground, used anciently for mortar and for waterproofing — the morter of Babel and the daubing of Moses’ ark.
webster_full: SLIME, a soft, viscous earth; in Scripture, bitumen or asphalt.
From the Saxon slīm, “slime, mire”; not pond scum but the pitch of the ground.
It seeps naturally from the earth in Shinar and about the vale of Siddim.
At Babel they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter (Gen 11:3).
With slime and pitch the ark of bulrushes was daubed for Moses (Exo 2:3).
scriptures: Gen 11:3
And they said one to another, Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly. And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter.
Gen 11:4
And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
Gen 11:9
Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth.
Exo 2:3
And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink.
corruption_summary: The live corruption is the reading of Babel as a charming tale that explains why men speak different tongues — instead of a real rebellion really judged, and man’s brick-and-slime project still going up.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live corruption here, and it comes wearing academic clothes: Babel read as a pleasant tale invented after the fact to explain why men speak different tongues — a story about language rather than a rebellion against God. Moses is not writing a fable. He names the plain of Shinar, the building material, the mortar, the purpose, and the LORD’s own descent and judgment; and Genesis hangs the whole table of the nations on it. The details are the details of a builder: brick because Shinar has no stone, slime because Shinar has bitumen. To dissolve that into a story is to take from the church a real judgment on a real sin, and to leave in its place a curiosity. Archaeology may confirm the brick and the bitumen of the Mesopotamian ziggurats; it does not sit in judgment on the Word that told us about them. The canonical narrative is the authority, and the spade is the corroborating witness.

The deeper corruption is the project itself, and it has never stopped. Brick for stone and slime for morter: a manufactured substitute for what God gives, mortared with what men scrape off the ground, raised to reach heaven and to make us a name. That is the religion of the natural heart in one sentence — a stair built upward by human hands, so that we may arrive at God on our terms and be famous for it. And the LORD came down. He always must; the tower never reaches. Yet mark the mercy hidden in the same black pitch: the slime that mortared Babel also daubed the little ark of bulrushes that carried Moses over the water of a king’s decree. God takes the very stuff of man’s self-salvation and uses it to save His own. We do not climb to Him; He comes down — at Babel to scatter, at Bethlehem to redeem.
roots_summary: The word means bitumen or asphalt, the natural pitch of the ground used as mortar.
roots_lines: Slime — Old English slīm, “slime, mire.”
In Scripture it renders the Hebrew for bitumen or asphalt, not pond scum.
It seeps from the ground in Shinar and about the vale of Siddim.
At Babel it was the morter of man’s self-made tower (Gen 11:3).
It also daubed the ark of bulrushes that preserved Moses (Exo 2:3).
usage: They had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter — man’s own stair to heaven.
Let us make us a name: Babel’s slime is the mortar of every self-salvation project.
The same slime daubed the ark of bulrushes: God uses the pitch of the earth to save.

etymology: An older form of marsh, from the Old French maresc and the Old English mersc, “a marsh, a fen”; hence low, standing, boggy ground. A KJV hapax, occurring but once, in the plural.
biblical_def: A marish is a marsh — low ground where water lies still and will not run, a fen, a bog. The word occurs once only in all Scripture, and it stands in the great river-vision of Ezekiel: “But the miry places thereof and the marishes thereof shall not be healed; they shall be given to salt” (Eze 47:11). The prophet had watched the waters issue from under the threshold of the house of God and deepen from the ankles to the loins until they could not be passed over, and everywhere that river came it made alive: “every thing that liveth, which moveth… shall live… for they shall be healed” (Eze 47:9). Even the dead salt sea was made fresh. And then this exception. The marishes are the places the river reaches but does not run through — the standing pools and swamps beside the living stream, which take the water in and hold it and let it stagnate, and are given to salt. The picture is severe and exact. The gospel goes out from the sanctuary and heals whatever it flows through; but the man who lets the Word stand in him without moving him — who hears the river and never joins it, who lies beside the stream and rots — is not healed by nearness. The marish drank the same water as the healed places. It is given to salt still, a barren ground within sight of the river of God.
webster_summary: An old form of marsh: low, boggy ground where water stands and does not run. A KJV hapax, in Ezekiel’s river-vision.
webster_full: MARISH, a marsh; a fen; a bog; low ground covered with standing water.
An older form of marsh, from Old French maresc, Old English mersc.
It occurs but once in Scripture, a KJV hapax (Eze 47:11).
In the temple vision, the marishes are the places not healed by the river.
They are given to salt — barren ground beside the water of life.
scriptures: But the miry places thereof and the marishes thereof shall not be healed; they shall be given to salt.
Eze 47:9

And it shall come to pass, that every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live: and there shall be a very great multitude of fish, because these waters shall come thither: for they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh.

And by the river upon the bank thereof, on this side and on that side, shall grow all trees for meat, whose leaf shall not fade, neither shall the fruit thereof be consumed: it shall bring forth new fruit according to his months, because their waters they issued out of the sanctuary: and the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine.
Lev 2:13

And every oblation of thy meat offering shalt thou season with salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat offering: with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old word for a marsh; it recovers a solemn exception in the river-vision — nearness to the water of life is not the same as being healed by it.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the presumption of proximity. Ezekiel’s river issues from under the threshold of the sanctuary and heals whatever it touches — ankles, knees, loins, waters to swim in, trees for meat on either bank, a multitude of fish in the sea that was dead. And then, in the middle of all that life, one flat sentence: the miry places and the marishes shall not be healed; they shall be given to salt. The marish is not far from the river. It is right beside it. It has the same water in it. But the water does not run through a marish; it stands, and stagnates, and the ground stays salt. To sit under the preaching of the Word for thirty years, and take it in, and never let it move you through, is to be a marish beside the river of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the fault is never in the river. The waters issued out of the sanctuary; wherever the river cometh, every thing shall live. The healing is in the stream, not in the soil, and the marish is condemned not because the water failed but because it would not move. Let no man comfort himself that he lives in a Christian house, keeps a Christian calendar, and has heard a thousand sermons. The question is not whether the river has come near you but whether it runs through you and out of you, so that trees grow on your banks whose leaf shall not fade and whose fruit is meat and medicine to others. Standing water goes to salt; running water carries life.
roots_summary: The word means a marsh — low, boggy ground where water stands and does not run.
roots_lines: Marish — an older form of marsh, Old French maresc.
From the Old English mersc, “a marsh, a fen.”
It denotes low ground where the water lies still and will not run.
A KJV hapax, occurring but once (Eze 47:11).
In the temple vision the marishes are not healed, but given to salt.
usage: The miry places and the marishes shall not be healed — a marsh beside the river of God.
A marish holds the water without moving: standing water goes to salt.
Wherever the river runs, every thing liveth; where it merely stands, the ground stays barren.

etymology: From the Old French champagne, “open country,” from the Latin campania (campus, “a field”); hence flat, open, level ground without wood or hill. A KJV hapax; it has nothing to do with the wine of that name.
biblical_def: A champaign is open country — a flat, level plain, unbroken by wood or hill, where a man can see a long way and be seen. It occurs once in the KJV, and the place it marks matters: Moses points the people toward Gerizim and Ebal, “in the land of the Canaanites, which dwell in the champaign over against Gilgal, beside the plains of Moreh” (Deu 11:30). This is the geography of covenant. The people are about to cross Jordan; and the LORD appoints that when they come in they shall “put the blessing upon mount Gerizim, and the curse upon mount Ebal” (Deu 11:29). Joshua did it exactly: all Israel, elders and officers and judges, the stranger as well as the home-born, stood half over against Gerizim and half over against Ebal with the ark and the Levites between, and the blessings and the cursings of the law were read aloud in the open (Jos 8:33). At Gilgal in the same open country they had already kept the passover in the plains of Jericho (Jos 5:10). The champaign is the theatre God chose for this. A covenant is not made in a corner. The blessing and the curse were set before the whole nation on level ground where every eye could see the two mountains and every ear could hear the law — because God deals with His people openly, and the terms He offers are public terms, plainly told, with nothing hidden in the hills.
webster_summary: Open, flat, level country without wood or hill; a plain. A KJV hapax, naming the open ground over against Gilgal.
webster_full: CHAMPAIGN, a flat, open country; level ground; a plain without wood or hill.
From Old French champagne, from Latin campania, “field, open country.”
It has no relation to the wine that bears a like name.
A KJV hapax, occurring but once (Deu 11:30).
It names the open ground over against Gilgal, by Gerizim and Ebal.
scriptures: Are they not on the other side Jordan, by the way where the sun goeth down, in the land of the Canaanites, which dwell in the champaign over against Gilgal, beside the plains of Moreh?

And it shall come to pass, when the LORD thy God hath brought thee in unto the land whither thou goest to possess it, that thou shalt put the blessing upon mount Gerizim, and the curse upon mount Ebal.
Jos 8:33

And all Israel, and their elders, and officers, and their judges, stood on this side the ark and on that side before the priests the Levites, which bare the ark of the covenant of the LORD, as well the stranger, as he that was born among them; half of them over against mount Gerizim, and half of them over against mount Ebal; as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded before, that they should bless the people of Israel.
Jos 5:10
And the children of Israel encamped in Gilgal, and kept the passover on the fourteenth day of the month at even in the plains of Jericho.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old word for open country; it recovers that God sets blessing and curse before His people in the open, on terms plainly told.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes a religion of the private and the vague. The LORD did not whisper His covenant to a committee; He appointed the champaign, the open plain over against Gilgal, with two mountains standing up on either hand, and there the blessing and the curse were set before the whole nation. Joshua carried it out to the letter — all Israel, elders, officers, judges, the stranger as well as the home-born, the ark and the Levites in the midst, and the law read aloud so that not a word was left out. God’s dealings with His people are open dealings. The terms are published; the blessing and the curse are both named; and no man on that plain could plead afterward that he had not been told.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plainness of God’s covenant terms. Level ground is honest ground: nothing hides in a champaign. If the LORD had meant to save on undisclosed conditions He would not have staged the reading between Gerizim and Ebal, where every eye saw both mountains at once. Blessing on the one hand for obedience; curse on the other for rebellion — and the gospel does not soften that arithmetic but satisfies it, for Christ was made a curse for us, hanging on a tree between heaven and earth in the open, that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles. The two mountains still stand. The Lamb has stood under one of them for His people.
roots_summary: The word means open, flat, level country — a plain without wood or hill.
roots_lines: Champaign — Old French champagne, “open country.”
From the Latin campania, from campus, “a field.”
It denotes flat, level ground, unbroken by wood or hill.
It bears no relation to the wine of the like name.
A KJV hapax, naming the plain over against Gilgal (Deu 11:30).
usage: The Canaanites dwelt in the champaign over against Gilgal — open, level, unhidden ground.
God set the blessing and the curse in the champaign, where every eye could see both mountains.
Nothing hides in a champaign: the covenant terms were published, not whispered.

etymology: From the Old English neoþera, “lower, further down,” comparative of niþer, “down”; hence lower, under, beneath — as the nether millstone lies under the upper.
biblical_def: Nether means lower — the under one, the thing beneath. The KJV uses it in three places, and each is worth knowing. It marks the foot of Sinai: “Moses brought forth the people out of the camp to meet with God; and they stood at the nether part of the mount” (Exo 19:17). The people met God at the bottom, under bounds, while the mountain smoked above them — nearness on God’s terms, not man’s. It marks a mercy in the law of pledges: “No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man’s life to pledge” (Deu 24:6). The nether millstone was the great fixed stone on which the upper turned; take either and the family cannot grind, and a creditor who seizes the mill has seized the bread. And it marks the place of the dead: Ezekiel’s dirge over the tall tree brings the proud down “to the nether parts of the earth” (Eze 31:16), to lie among the uncircumcised with them that be slain by the sword (Eze 31:18). The word therefore teaches direction. Man’s instinct is upward — the tower, the tall tree, the top among the thick boughs. God’s answer to every such height is the nether parts of the earth; and His way up is down, for the Lord who descended is the same also that ascended far above all heavens.
webster_summary: Lower; under; lying beneath — as the nether millstone under the upper, the nether part of the mount, the nether parts of the earth.
webster_full: NETHER, lower; lying beneath or under; opposed to upper.
From the Saxon neoþera, “lower,” from niþer, “down.”
The nether millstone is the fixed stone on which the upper turns (Deu 24:6).
Israel stood at the nether part of the mount to meet with God (Exo 19:17).
The nether parts of the earth are the place of the dead (Eze 31:16).
scriptures: And Moses brought forth the people out of the camp to meet with God; and they stood at the nether part of the mount.
Deu 24:6
No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man's life to pledge.

I made the nations to shake at the sound of his fall, when I cast him down to hell with them that descend into the pit: and all the trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon, all that drink water, shall be comforted in the nether parts of the earth.

To whom art thou thus like in glory and in greatness among the trees of Eden? yet shalt thou be brought down with the trees of Eden unto the nether parts of the earth: thou shalt lie in the midst of the uncircumcised with them that be slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, saith the Lord GOD.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the plain old word for lower; it recovers that God brings every proud height down to the nether parts, and that His way up is down.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the creditor who forgets he is dealing with a life. God legislated the nether millstone: no man shall take the nether or the upper to pledge, for he taketh a man’s life to pledge. A mill is not furniture; it is the household’s bread, and a lender who carries off either stone has not secured a debt, he has stopped a family’s eating. The LORD writes that into His law and gives the reason, so that no man can plead the letter of a contract against the life of his neighbour. There is a whole doctrine of lending in one clause: a debt may be collected, but never out of the means by which the debtor lives.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the direction God has fixed for pride. Ezekiel’s tall tree shot up his top among the thick boughs and was fair in his greatness, and every tree of Eden envied him — and the LORD brought him down to the nether parts of the earth, to lie with the uncircumcised and them that be slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh, says the prophet; and it is Babel’s tower, and every height men raise for themselves. But mark the opposite motion in the gospel: Israel met God at the nether part of the mount, at the bottom, under bounds, because sinners cannot climb to Him — and Christ came down to the nether parts Himself, that He might raise His people up. Whoso exalteth himself shall be abased, and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
roots_summary: The word means lower, under, lying beneath — the opposite of upper.
roots_lines: Nether — Old English neoþera, “lower, further down.”
From niþer, “down”; it is the comparative of downward.
The nether millstone is the fixed stone under the turning upper (Deu 24:6).
The nether part of the mount is its foot, where Israel stood (Exo 19:17).
The nether parts of the earth are the pit, the place of the dead (Eze 31:16).
usage: No man shall take the nether millstone to pledge: he taketh a man’s life to pledge.
Israel stood at the nether part of the mount — near to God, but under bounds He set.
The tall tree of Eden was brought down to the nether parts: God’s answer to every height.

etymology: The past participle of dandle, of uncertain origin, akin to the Italian dandolare, “to dandle, to trifle”; to move a little child up and down upon the knee or in the arms in play and fondness. A KJV hapax.
biblical_def: To dandle is to bounce a little child gently upon the knee — the tender, playful, wholly unnecessary fondness of a mother with an infant who is already fed and already safe. The word occurs once in Scripture, at the very close of Isaiah, in the LORD’s last great promise to Zion: “Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the Gentiles like a flowing stream: then shall ye suck, ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees” (Isa 66:12). The figure is Jerusalem as a mother and her restored people as her nursing children, satisfied with the breasts of her consolations (Isa 66:11), carried on the hip, bounced on the knee. And then the LORD applies it to Himself in a simile: “As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem” (Isa 66:13). This is one of the most tender sentences in the prophets. God does not merely pardon His people, provide for them, and dismiss them; He comforts them as a mother comforts — the same word He uses when He says of Israel, can a woman forget her sucking child? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee (Isa 49:15). The Shepherd who gathers the lambs with His arm carries them in His bosom (Isa 40:11). The God whose peace comes like a river stoops to dandle His children on His knee.
webster_summary: Dandled: bounced gently upon the knee, as a mother plays with an infant. A KJV hapax, in the LORD’s promise of motherly comfort to Zion.
webster_full: DANDLE, to move a little child up and down in the arms or on the knee.
To fondle, to play with an infant in tenderness.
Of uncertain origin; akin to the Italian dandolare, “to dandle.”
A KJV hapax, occurring only as the participle dandled (Isa 66:12).
In Isaiah, the restored people are dandled upon the knees of Zion.
scriptures: For thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the Gentiles like a flowing stream: then shall ye suck, ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees.
As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.
Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.
He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.
corruption_summary: The live corruption is the feminist reimagining of God as Mother built on Isa 66:13; the text gives a comparison, not a name, and a simile is not a title.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live corruption here, and it must be named. Isa 66:13 — “As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you” — has been made the chief proof-text of the feminist theology that would rename God as Mother, address Him as She, and recast the Fatherhood of the first Person as a cultural accident of an ancient people rather than revelation. The text will not bear it, and the reason is grammar before it is doctrine. Isaiah does not say God is a mother. He says God comforts as a mother comforts. That is a simile, a comparison of one action to another, and a comparison is not a name. Scripture compares the LORD to a lion, an eagle, a rock, a moth, a bear robbed of her whelps, a husbandman, a refiner’s fire; no one proposes that we address Him as Rock or pray to our Eagle in heaven. The whole prophecy is drenched in the point: the same verse says the comfort will be given “in Jerusalem,” and no one argues from that phrase that God is a city.

The corrective is to let Scripture set its own titles. God has named Himself, and He has done it with unwavering consistency: the LORD, the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; and the Son taught His disciples to pray “Our Father, which art in heaven,” not to choose their own address for the Almighty. The pronouns Scripture uses of God are masculine from Genesis to Revelation, and the eternal relations of Father and Son are not borrowed from human sociology — human fatherhood is named from His, not He from ours. To rename God is not to enrich our devotion; it is to worship a god of our own making, which is idolatry however tender the motive. And nothing whatever is lost by refusing it. The Father who will not be called Mother is the very One who says He will comfort us as a mother comforts, extend peace to us like a river, carry us in His bosom, and dandle us upon His knees. The doctrine is not cold. It is only true.
roots_summary: The word means to bounce or fondle a little child upon the knee or in the arms.
roots_lines: Dandle — of uncertain origin, akin to Italian dandolare, “to dandle.”
It denotes moving an infant up and down on the knee in fondness and play.
A KJV hapax, occurring only as the participle dandled (Isa 66:12).
In Isaiah, Zion’s children are borne on her sides and dandled on her knees.
The LORD likens His comfort to a mother’s — a simile, not a name (Isa 66:13).
usage: Ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees — Zion’s nursing children.
As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you: a comparison, not a title.
The God who extends peace like a river stoops to dandle His children on His knee.
